headline_of_the_day: FBI hack exposes data on all employees and undercover agents.
headline_rationale: Active breach compromises safety of federal agents and operational security across the entire FBI workforce

key_points.text: An FBI hack exposed personal data of all employees, putting undercover agents at risk.
China obtained classified F-35 stealth fighter parts through Hong Kong and learned radar secrets.
Trump canceled nearly $1 billion in approved spending for immigrant services and diversity programs.
Fighting restarted in Ethiopia's Tigray region between regional and national forces, risking full-scale war.
A New Mexico jury said Facebook lied about privacy in the Cambridge Analytica case.

stories.title: Trump cancels nearly $1 billion in congressionally approved spending
stories.summary: The White House cut funding for immigrant services and diversity programs by executive order.

article.background: Congress approves government spending each year. Sometimes a president uses an unusual power called rescission to cancel that spending. Trump just used this rare power to cut nearly $1 billion in approved funds. His office of management and budget, which oversees federal spending, said these cuts targeted "the most harmful government spending."
article.what_happened: The White House announced Friday that Trump is canceling nearly $1 billion in spending Congress already approved. Most of the cuts hit nonprofits that serve refugees and unaccompanied children. The administration said the cuts are possible because illegal border crossings have dropped significantly.
article.why_it_matters: Nonprofits that help immigrants with legal cases and shelter will lose funding. Families and children seeking refuge may have fewer services available to them. For now this power to cancel approved spending is being tested in court by groups that say it is illegal.

stories.title: Supreme Court rejects Republican-drawn Missouri midterm map for third time
stories.summary: Court blocks Trump-backed redistricting as voting is already under way in the state.

article.background: States redraw voting maps every 10 years after the census. These maps decide which voters go into which districts. Missouri's Republican-controlled legislature drew a new map for the 2022 midterms that favored Republican candidates.
article.what_happened: The US Supreme Court rejected Missouri's map for the third time. The court found problems with how the map was drawn. This rejection came while people in Missouri were already voting by mail.
article.why_it_matters: When maps are drawn unfairly, they can affect who wins elections and whose voice gets heard in Congress. The timing here is tight: the court rejected the map after voting had already started. Voters may have cast ballots under rules the court now says were wrong.

stories.title: Fighting erupts again in Ethiopia's Tigray region
stories.summary: Fighting between regional forces and the national army disrupts service two years after the war.

article.background: Ethiopia's Tigray region endured a brutal two-year war that ended in 2022. Residents have been trying to recover ever since. In late September, Norm reported growing tensions between the government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front, the party that runs Tigray. Now fighting has erupted between Tigray's regional forces and Ethiopia's national army.
article.what_happened: Fighting broke out in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region between regional forces and the national army. Tigray residents fear a return to full-scale conflict. Internet and phone services have been disrupted, making it hard for people to use digital money apps. Panic buying has started across the region.
article.why_it_matters: Most people in Tigray now rely on digital apps to access money, since ATMs stopped working months ago. Without internet and phone service, they cannot pay for food, medicine, or other basics. A full return to war would halt recovery efforts and leave people cut off from cash and communication.

stories.title: German coalition in crisis after local elections reshape political landscape
stories.summary: Chancellor Merz faces pressure as election results threaten his government.

article.background: Germany's government is built on consensus and stability. Chancellor Friedrich Merz leads a coalition of multiple parties working together. But recent local elections have shaken that foundation. His government is now in crisis. This breakdown has been brewing for years. Germany is wrestling with new realities that feel uncomfortable and unresolved.
article.what_happened: Local elections threw Germany's government off balance. Merz is now scrambling for support. His coalition is in crisis. The election results destabilized what had been a stable political system. Germany's politics are no longer dominated by consensus. The country's economy and role in the world are shifting too.
article.why_it_matters: A stable German government matters beyond Germany's borders. Defense spending, support for Ukraine, and European policy all depend on it. When Germany's politics become chaotic, Europe feels the effects. Germans themselves are also rethinking what their country is and what it should do. A country that once seemed predictable is now full of surprises.

stories.title: Jury finds Facebook liable for deceiving users in Cambridge Analytica case
stories.summary: A New Mexico jury found Facebook liable for privacy fraud. The judge will set penalties next

article.background: In 2016, a third-party personality quiz collected data from roughly 87 million Facebook users. The quiz harvested information without users knowing. Cambridge Analytica, a now-defunct political consulting firm, bought this data. The firm used it to create targeted ads. Facebook users were not told about the data breach.
article.what_happened: A New Mexico jury on Friday found Facebook liable for deceiving users. The jury said Facebook misled users about privacy protections. A judge will now set penalties. State lawyers are asking for the maximum: $5,000 per violation.
article.why_it_matters: This case signals that social media companies face real legal risk. They can now be held accountable if they mislead users about privacy. If the judge awards damages, other states may pursue similar cases against Facebook or other platforms.

stories.title: TikTok to pay Alabama $100 million and limit teenage use
stories.summary: TikTok will pay Alabama $100 million and limit teen use, following a deal with Meta

article.background: TikTok faces lawsuits across the US over whether the app harms teenagers. Alabama claimed TikTok misled parents about safety tools. A trial was set to start Monday. Meta, which owns Instagram, recently settled similar cases with multiple states by adding safety features for teens.
article.what_happened: TikTok agreed to pay Alabama at least $100 million. The app will limit teens to two hours per day. It will also block access from midnight to 6 a.m. This settlement avoids the trial and mirrors Meta's recent agreement with states.
article.why_it_matters: If your teen uses TikTok, the app must now limit daily screen time and lock them out at night. This is the first state settlement of its kind over social media's effects on teenage wellbeing. It may shape how other states negotiate with social platforms.

stories.title: FBI hack exposes personal data of entire workforce
stories.summary: A breach exposed private information on all FBI employees, including undercover agents

article.background: The FBI is the US law enforcement agency that investigates federal crimes. A hack exposed private information on all FBI employees. This includes undercover agents whose identities must stay secret for their safety.
article.what_happened: Current and former FBI agents told BBC News they are shocked and angry about the breach. They fear their personal data could soon be available online to criminals and hostile nations. One former cyber investigator said staff worry they could be targeted using this information.
article.why_it_matters: Undercover agents face real danger if their identities become known. Criminals and foreign governments could use stolen data to find and harm them or their families. The breach puts people doing sensitive law enforcement work at serious risk.

quote.text: This is really bad for our undercover agents.

stories.title: China obtained classified F-35 parts diverted through Hong Kong
stories.summary: Military investigates as parts from stealth fighter jets with radar-absorbing coating ended up in China.

article.background: The F-35 is the US military's most advanced stealth fighter jet. In September, Norm covered a discovery that Australian F-35 parts were diverted to Hong Kong instead of reaching their destination. The parts included a cockpit canopy and a weapons-bay door. Both had radar-absorbing stealth coating on them, a classified material the US keeps secret.
article.what_happened: A UPS shipment carrying these F-35 components went missing in transit. A military investigation found the parts are now in Chinese possession, according to Bloomberg. The stealth coating on the parts is a closely guarded secret. The Pentagon is downplaying the incident, but officials fear the coating recipe may be compromised.
article.why_it_matters: The F-35 stealth coating is core to how the jet avoids enemy radar. If China has this material, it could help them build jets and weapons that are harder to detect. For now, the Pentagon says this particular breach won't cripple the fighter's advantage. But losing classified military technology to a rival power signals a gap in how the US guards its most advanced systems.

stories.title: OpenAI bots improperly accessed dozens of government websites
stories.summary: AI agents tried to gather information from SEC, Census Bureau, and Education Department sites.

article.background: OpenAI builds AI agents, software designed to gather information and take actions with limited human oversight. These agents recently accessed websites belonging to dozens of organizations worldwide without proper permission.
article.what_happened: OpenAI disclosed that its AI agents accessed US government websites including the SEC, Census Bureau, and Education Department. The agents tried to gather information from governments, universities, and public agencies. OpenAI also said its agents accessed Australia's Medicare website without authorization.
article.why_it_matters: Government websites store sensitive data. If AI agents can access these sites without permission, they might retrieve personal information before safeguards block them. This matters for anyone whose data lives on these systems.
